The invention concerns an apparatus for determining the relationship between motion at the surface of a body and motion of an object located within that body. Such an apparatus may be used, for example, in medical or interventional procedures in which movement of an internal organ, tissue region, target structure, or other internal object is influenced by or correlated with externally observable motion, such as respiratory motion at the body surface.

The apparatus comprises a first sensing unit configured to acquire a first position signal from a first element positioned on the surface of the body. The first element is placed at a location where surface motion occurs, so that the first position signal represents the movement of the body surface over time. This surface motion may correspond, for instance, to chest or abdominal movement caused by breathing.

The apparatus further comprises a second sensing unit configured to acquire a second position signal from a second element. The second element is attached to an interventional device and is positioned on or within the object inside the body. The second position signal therefore represents the motion of the internal object, or of a point associated with the internal object, during the same time period.

The first and second sensing units are arranged to acquire their respective position signals synchronously over a predetermined or selected duration. By obtaining the surface-motion signal and the internal-object-motion signal at the same time, the apparatus enables a direct comparison between the two motions and allows temporal correlations, delays, amplitudes, phases, or other motion characteristics to be identified.

A third unit is provided for calculating the relationship between the surface motion and the motion of the object based on the first and second position signals. This calculation may include determining a correlation, transformation, model, mapping function, or other mathematical relation that describes how movement detected at the body surface corresponds to movement of the internal object. The resulting relation can be used to estimate or predict the position of the internal object from subsequent measurements of the surface motion, thereby supporting accurate monitoring, navigation, targeting, or compensation for internal motion during a procedure.
outputs.L4:
An apparatus and method are provided for determining a motion relationship between movement of an external surface of a body and movement of an internal object located within the body. The apparatus includes a first position-sensing element configured to be placed on or near the surface of the body, such as on the skin of a patient, and a second position-sensing element configured to be attached to, integrated with, or otherwise associated with an interventional device positioned on, in, or adjacent to the internal object. The internal object may be, for example, an organ, tissue region, lesion, tumor, vessel, anatomical landmark, or treatment target whose position varies as a result of breathing, cardiac motion, patient movement, or other physiological activity.

During operation, position signals are acquired from both the first element and the second element in a synchronized manner. The first position signal represents motion of the body surface, while the second position signal represents motion of the interventional device and, consequently, motion of the internal object with which the device is associated. Synchronization of the signals may be performed by simultaneous sampling, time-stamping, common triggering, or another timing coordination technique, so that corresponding surface and internal positions can be compared accurately over time.

The acquired signals are processed to determine a relation between the surface motion and the internal object motion. This relation may include, for example, a displacement correlation, phase relationship, time delay, amplitude scaling factor, motion model, or mathematical transformation that maps the measured surface movement to the corresponding internal movement. In some implementations, the relation may be determined by fitting a model to the synchronized position data, by statistical correlation, by regression analysis, or by adaptive learning techniques that update the relation as additional motion data is obtained.

Once established, the motion relation enables external body surface movement to be used as an indicator of internal object movement. This allows the position of the internal object to be estimated, predicted, monitored, or compensated for based on the more readily obtainable surface motion signal. The technique may be used in image-guided intervention, radiation therapy, surgical navigation, biopsy, catheter placement, ablation, or other medical procedures in which it is desirable to correlate external motion with internal anatomical motion. By using synchronized measurements from a surface-placed element and an element associated with an interventional device, the apparatus and method provide an improved basis for tracking internal motion and for coordinating diagnostic or therapeutic actions with the movement of the body.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps us refer to something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we are not talking about any book, but a particular book that the speaker and listener understand.

Although “the” may seem simple, it gives clarity and meaning to sentences. It can point to a unique object, such as “the sun,” or something already mentioned, like “I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.” Without this word, English would often sound unclear or incomplete.

In everyday language, “the” appears everywhere: in conversations, books, news, songs, and titles. Its frequent use shows how important small words can be. Even though “the” is short, it helps organize ideas and make communication precise. This makes “the” a quiet but powerful part of the English language.

## Description

### Title

**Apparatus and method for determining a relationship between motion at a body surface and motion of an object within the body**

### Technical Field

The invention relates to an apparatus and a method for determining how motion at at least one location on a surface of a body relates to motion of an object within the body. The invention is particularly, but not exclusively, applicable to medical imaging, radiotherapy, image-guided intervention, respiratory motion compensation, and patient monitoring.

### Background

In a number of medical and technical applications it is desirable to know the position or motion of an object located inside a body. For example, in radiotherapy a tumour or another target region may move due to respiration, cardiac activity, peristalsis, patient movement, or other physiological motion. Since continuous direct imaging of the internal object may be impractical, expensive, or associated with undesired radiation exposure, external motion signals measured at the body surface are often used as surrogate signals.

Known systems may monitor the motion of markers attached to the skin, optical surface points, belts, pressure sensors, or other external indicators. However, the relationship between the external surface motion and the internal object motion is often patient-specific, time-dependent, non-linear, and may vary between different regions of the body surface. A simple assumption that a surface marker motion directly corresponds to internal object motion may therefore lead to inaccurate position estimation.

There is thus a need for an apparatus and method capable of determining, for a particular body or patient, how motion at one or more body surface locations relates to motion of an internal object, so that the internal object motion may be estimated or predicted from surface motion.

### Summary

It is an object of the invention to provide an improved apparatus and method for determining a relationship between motion at a location on a body surface and motion of an object within the body.

According to an aspect, an apparatus is provided comprising at least one surface sensing unit configured to sense motion at at least one location on a surface of a body, at least one object sensing unit configured to sense motion of an object within the body, and a calculation unit configured to determine, on the basis of the sensed surface motion and the sensed object motion, relationship information indicating how the motion at the at least one surface location relates to the motion of the object.

The relationship information may comprise a correlation, a transformation, a transfer function, a mathematical model, a regression model, a mapping, a time delay, a phase relationship, a scaling factor, a confidence value, or any combination thereof. The relationship information may be used subsequently to estimate the object motion from surface motion sensed by the surface sensing unit, optionally without continuously sensing the object directly.

According to a further aspect, a corresponding method is provided, comprising sensing motion at at least one location on a surface of a body, sensing motion of an object within the body, and determining, based on the sensed motions, relationship information indicating how the surface motion relates to the object motion.

### Brief Description of the Drawings

Embodiments of the invention will now be described with reference to the following schematic drawings.

**Fig. 1** schematically shows an apparatus for determining relationship information between surface motion and internal object motion.

**Fig. 2** schematically shows a body having a plurality of surface sensing locations and an internal object.

**Fig. 3** schematically shows a processing flow for determining and using relationship information.

**Fig. 4** schematically shows an embodiment in which relationship information is updated over time.

### Detailed Description of Embodiments

Fig. 1 schematically shows an apparatus 1 for determining a relationship between motion at a body surface 3 and motion of an object 5 within a body 2. The body 2 may be a human or animal body. The object 5 may be an anatomical structure, a lesion, a tumour, an organ, a vessel, a bone structure, an implanted marker, a surgical instrument, a catheter, or another internal object whose motion is to be determined or monitored.

The apparatus 1 comprises one or more surface sensing units 10, one or more object sensing units 20, and a calculation unit 30. The surface sensing unit 10 is configured to sense motion at at least one location 4 on the surface 3 of the body 2. The object sensing unit 20 is configured to sense motion of the object 5 within the body 2. The calculation unit 30 is configured to receive surface motion data from the surface sensing unit 10 and object motion data from the object sensing unit 20 and to determine relationship information 40 indicating how the surface motion relates to the object motion.

The term “motion” as used herein may include displacement, velocity, acceleration, deformation, rotation, periodic motion, quasi-periodic motion, respiratory motion, cardiac motion, or any other time-varying change in position or shape. Motion may be represented in one, two, or three spatial dimensions and may be expressed relative to a coordinate system of the apparatus, a patient support, an imaging system, or the body.

#### Surface sensing unit

The surface sensing unit 10 may comprise any sensor capable of providing information about motion at the body surface 3. In one embodiment, the surface sensing unit 10 comprises an optical sensing system, for example one or more cameras, depth cameras, structured-light sensors, stereo cameras, infrared cameras, laser scanners, time-of-flight cameras, or surface imaging devices. The optical sensing system may track natural skin features, projected patterns, or markers attached to the surface 3.

In another embodiment, the surface sensing unit 10 comprises one or more contact sensors, such as accelerometers, strain sensors, displacement sensors, pressure sensors, capacitive sensors, inductive sensors, fibre-optic sensors, magnetic sensors, or respiratory belts. The contact sensors may be attached to the skin or to clothing, or may be integrated into a support surface.

In a further embodiment, the surface sensing unit 10 comprises a plurality of sensing elements arranged to detect surface motion at a plurality of surface locations 4a, 4b, 4c, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The plurality of surface locations may be distributed over a thorax, abdomen, back, head, limb, or other body region. The calculation unit 30 may determine which of the surface locations has the strongest, most stable, or otherwise most suitable relationship to the motion of the object 5.

The surface motion data may comprise a time series of positions, displacements, velocities, amplitudes, phases, surface maps, deformation fields, marker coordinates, or sensor signal values. The surface sensing unit 10 may further comprise a preprocessing unit configured to filter noise, compensate for drift, remove outliers, correct for rigid body motion, or transform the sensed motion into a common coordinate system.

#### Object sensing unit

The object sensing unit 20 is configured to sense motion of the internal object 5. The object sensing unit 20 may comprise an imaging device, such as an ultrasound imaging device, X-ray imaging device, fluoroscopy device, computed tomography device, magnetic resonance imaging device, positron emission tomography device, single photon emission computed tomography device, optical coherence tomography device, or another internal imaging modality.

Alternatively or additionally, the object sensing unit 20 may comprise a tracking device configured to track an implanted or inserted marker, transponder, electromagnetic sensor, radioactive seed, acoustic marker, magnetic marker, or other fiducial associated with the object 5. The object sensing unit 20 may also be configured to derive the object motion from a sequence of images by segmentation, registration, feature tracking, template matching, or other image-processing technique.

The object motion data may comprise a time series of object positions, centre-of-mass positions, fiducial positions, deformation fields, object contours, object orientations, or object velocities. In some embodiments the object sensing unit 20 senses the object motion only during a calibration period, whereas the surface sensing unit 10 continues to sense the surface motion during a subsequent monitoring or treatment period.

#### Calculation unit

The calculation unit 30 may comprise one or more processors, computers, controllers, programmable logic devices, graphics processing units, cloud-based computing resources, or any other suitable data-processing circuitry. The calculation unit 30 may be connected to the surface sensing unit 10 and the object sensing unit 20 by wired or wireless communication links.

The calculation unit 30 is configured to temporally associate the surface motion data with the object motion data. For example, the calculation unit 30 may receive time stamps, trigger signals, clock signals, or synchronization data from the sensing units 10, 20. If the surface motion data and object motion data are acquired at different sampling rates, the calculation unit 30 may resample, interpolate, average, or otherwise align the data.

The calculation unit 30 determines relationship information 40 from the temporally associated data. The relationship information 40 may define a mapping:

\[
\mathbf{x}_{obj}(t) = F(\mathbf{x}_{surf}(t), \mathbf{x}_{surf}(t-\tau), \dot{\mathbf{x}}_{surf}(t), p)
\]

where \(\mathbf{x}_{obj}(t)\) represents the position or motion state of the object 5, \(\mathbf{x}_{surf}(t)\) represents the position or motion state at one or more surface locations, \(\tau\) represents a time delay, and \(p\) represents model parameters.

In one embodiment, the calculation unit 30 determines a linear relationship between the surface motion and the object motion. For example, the object displacement may be expressed as a weighted sum of displacements at a plurality of surface locations:

\[
\Delta \mathbf{x}_{obj}(t) = \sum_i w_i \Delta \mathbf{x}_{surf,i}(t-\tau_i) + \mathbf{b}
\]

where \(w_i\) are weighting factors, \(\tau_i\) are time delays, and \(\mathbf{b}\) is an offset.

In another embodiment, the calculation unit 30 determines a non-linear relationship using polynomial regression, splines, kernel methods, neural networks, random forests, Gaussian process regression, state-space models, Kalman filtering, recurrent models, or another machine-learning or statistical model.

In another embodiment, the relationship information 40 comprises correlation information. The calculation unit 30 may calculate, for each of a plurality of surface locations, a correlation coefficient, mutual information value, phase coherence value, error metric, or prediction accuracy value between the surface motion and the object motion. Based on this calculation, the apparatus 1 may identify a preferred surface location or a preferred combination of surface locations for estimating the object motion.

The relationship information 40 may also comprise a hysteresis model. For example, in respiratory motion the object 5 may occupy different positions during inhalation and exhalation even for the same surface displacement. The calculation unit 30 may therefore use additional variables, such as surface velocity, respiratory phase, or motion history, to distinguish between different motion branches.

#### Determining a time delay

In an embodiment, the calculation unit 30 determines a temporal offset between the surface motion and the object motion. The temporal offset may represent a delay between motion at the surface and motion of the internal object. The calculation unit 30 may determine the temporal offset by maximizing cross-correlation, minimizing prediction error, comparing phases, or fitting a dynamic model. The relationship information 40 may include the determined temporal offset, and the apparatus 1 may compensate for the offset when estimating the object position.

#### Selection of surface location

In an embodiment shown in Fig. 2, the surface sensing unit 10 senses motion at a plurality of surface locations 4a, 4b, 4c. The calculation unit 30 determines respective relationship information for each surface location or for combinations of locations. The calculation unit 30 may select one or more surface locations having a relationship to the object motion satisfying a selection criterion.

The selection criterion may include a high correlation with the object motion, a low prediction error, a stable phase relationship, a low noise level, a high signal amplitude, a low susceptibility to non-respiratory movement, or a high confidence value. The selected location or locations may be displayed to a user, stored for later use, or used automatically for object motion estimation.

#### Use of the relationship information

After determining the relationship information 40, the apparatus 1 may use it to estimate the motion or position of the object 5 from newly sensed surface motion. Thus, the calculation unit 30 may operate in a calibration mode, in which both surface motion and object motion are sensed, and in an estimation mode, in which surface motion is sensed and the object motion is estimated using the previously determined relationship information.

In a radiotherapy embodiment, the estimated object position may be provided to a treatment control system. The treatment control system may gate radiation delivery, adapt a beam position, adapt a treatment plan, or generate a warning if the object is outside an allowed region. In an imaging embodiment, the estimated object motion may be used to compensate image acquisition or reconstruction. In an interventional embodiment, the estimated object motion may be used to guide an instrument or to display a predicted position of the object.

#### Updating of relationship information

Fig. 4 schematically shows an embodiment in which the relationship information 40 is updated over time. Since the relationship between surface motion and internal object motion may change due to patient relaxation, baseline drift, anatomical changes, sensor repositioning, or altered breathing pattern, the calculation unit 30 may periodically or continuously update the relationship information 40 when new object motion data are available.

The update may be performed by recalculating the model, adapting model parameters, applying recursive least squares, using a Kalman filter, updating a machine-learning model, or blending old and new relationship information. The calculation unit 30 may also determine a confidence measure indicating whether the current surface motion is within a range for which the relationship information is valid. If the confidence measure falls below a threshold, the apparatus 1 may request renewed object sensing, indicate a warning, or inhibit use of the estimated object motion.

#### Coordinate systems and calibration

The apparatus 1 may include a coordinate transformation unit, which may be part of the calculation unit 30, for transforming surface motion data and object motion data into a common coordinate system. The common coordinate system may be associated with the body 2, a patient table, an imaging device, a treatment device, or a room coordinate system.

Calibration markers, anatomical landmarks, registration procedures, or known geometrical relationships between the sensing units may be used to determine the coordinate transformation. The calculation unit 30 may compensate for rigid body displacement of the body 2 separately from local surface motion, thereby improving the relationship determination.

#### Output unit and storage unit

The apparatus 1 may further comprise an output unit 50 configured to output the relationship information 40, the estimated object motion, selected surface locations, confidence values, or warnings. The output unit 50 may comprise a display, a graphical user interface, a data interface, a treatment system interface, an imaging system interface, or a storage interface.

The apparatus 1 may further comprise a memory 60 configured to store surface motion data, object motion data, model parameters, calibration data, relationship information, patient-specific data, or historical data. Stored relationship information may be retrieved in a later session and optionally verified or updated.

### Method

A corresponding method for determining how motion at a body surface relates to motion of an object within the body comprises the following steps.

In a first step, motion at at least one location on a surface of a body is sensed by a surface sensing unit. The sensed motion may comprise displacement, velocity, acceleration, phase, amplitude, surface deformation, or marker movement.

In a second step, motion of an object within the body is sensed by an object sensing unit. The object may be an anatomical structure, tumour, organ, implanted marker, instrument, or other internal object. The object motion may be sensed by imaging, marker tracking, or another internal sensing technique.

In a third step, the sensed surface motion and the sensed object motion are temporally associated. This may include synchronizing, resampling, interpolating, filtering, registering, or transforming the sensed data into a common coordinate system.

In a fourth step, relationship information is determined from the associated surface motion and object motion. The relationship information indicates how the motion at the surface location relates to the motion of the object. The relationship information may include a correlation, mapping, transfer function, regression model, time delay, phase relationship, weighting factor, scaling factor, hysteresis model, or confidence value.

In an optional further step, motion at a plurality of surface locations is sensed and the method determines which of the plurality of surface locations, or which combination thereof, has a desired relationship to the object motion. The desired relationship may be selected on the basis of correlation strength, prediction accuracy, stability, signal quality, or confidence.

In an optional further step, the relationship information is used to estimate subsequent motion of the object from subsequently sensed surface motion. The object sensing unit may then be used less frequently, for example only for verification or updating.

In an optional further step, the relationship information is updated when additional object motion data become available. The method may further comprise determining a validity or confidence measure and issuing a warning when the surface motion no longer corresponds sufficiently to the determined relationship.

### Example embodiment

In one example embodiment, the body is a patient and the object is a tumour in the thoracic or abdominal region. A camera-based surface sensing unit measures motion of a plurality of points on the patient’s chest and abdomen during breathing. An X-ray or ultrasound imaging unit measures the tumour position during a calibration interval. The calculation unit synchronizes the camera data and imaging data and determines a patient-specific model mapping the surface motion to the tumour motion. The calculation unit identifies that a particular abdominal surface region has the lowest prediction error. During a subsequent treatment interval, the camera-based surface sensing unit continues to monitor the selected region, and the calculation unit estimates the tumour position using the patient-specific model. If the estimated tumour position deviates from a permitted range, a treatment control signal may be generated.

### Advantages

The apparatus and method allow a patient-specific or body-specific relationship between external surface motion and internal object motion to be determined. This may improve estimation of internal object position compared with using a fixed or assumed relationship. By using a plurality of surface locations, the apparatus may identify those locations that best represent the internal motion. By determining time delays, phase relationships, and hysteresis, the apparatus may account for complex physiological motion. The apparatus may reduce the need for continuous internal imaging and may therefore reduce radiation exposure, imaging time, or system complexity.
